chunks.text: The Columbian Exchange was the two-way transfer of plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia, set in motion by Christopher Columbus's voyages beginning in 1492. It linked two hemispheres that had been almost completely separated for roughly 12,000 years.

The Columbian Exchange is one of the most important developments in world history. It transformed what humans ate, how many of them there were, where they lived, and how the global economy worked, while also unleashing the worst demographic catastrophe in recorded human history.

For thousands of years the peoples of the Americas lived in isolation from Afro-Eurasia and had never been exposed to Old World diseases such as smallpox, measles, influenza, and typhus. They had no inherited immunity, while Old World populations had developed partial resistance over millennia.

When Europeans arrived, Old World diseases swept through Native American populations who had no immunity, killing an estimated 80 to 90 percent within a century or two of contact. Historians call this the 'Great Dying'; the death toll ran into the tens of millions, the largest demographic disaster in recorded history.

The overwhelming cause of the Native American population collapse was disease, not war or massacre. Smallpox and other epidemics often raced ahead of the Europeans themselves, killing people who had never even seen a European, against whom Native peoples were biologically defenseless.

The demographic collapse had enormous consequences: it helped a few hundred Spanish conquistadors topple the Aztec and Inca empires as epidemics devastated populations and leadership, and the loss of indigenous labor drove Europeans to import enslaved Africans, fueling the Atlantic slave trade.

From the Americas to Afro-Eurasia traveled new foods including maize (corn), potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava (manioc), tomatoes, chili peppers, cacao (chocolate), peanuts, and tobacco. Before 1492, none of these existed outside the Americas.

From Afro-Eurasia to the Americas came wheat, rice, sugarcane, bananas, citrus fruits, coffee, and grapes, along with domesticated animals the Americas had largely lacked: horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, and chickens.

American crops were often highly nutritious and could grow in soils where Old World staples could not. The potato thrived in cold, poor European soils, and maize and sweet potatoes spread across China and Africa, allowing cultivation of marginal land. Historians link the early-modern global population surge substantially to these crops.

A striking paradox of the Columbian Exchange is that the same event that annihilated the population of the Americas through disease helped grow the population of Afro-Eurasia through new, nutritious American crops like the potato and maize.

Horses, which had gone extinct in the Americas long before, were reintroduced by the Spanish and transformed many Native American peoples, especially on the Great Plains of North America, where groups adopted horses for hunting bison and for warfare, creating powerful new mobile cultures.

The potato was domesticated in the Andes and was a staple of Inca civilization. After 1492 it spread to Europe, growing well in cool, poor northern soils and producing more calories per acre than grain, fueling population growth from Ireland to Russia.

Ireland became so dependent on the potato that when a blight destroyed the crop in the 1840s, the result was the catastrophic Irish Potato Famine, causing mass starvation and emigration. It shows how the Columbian Exchange created dangerous new dependencies.

European colonizers found that Old World sugarcane grew superbly in the American tropics and could be sold for huge profit. It was grown on plantations, large estates producing a single cash crop for export, in the Caribbean and Brazil, alongside tobacco, coffee, and cotton.

Plantations had a voracious appetite for labor. After the Great Dying destroyed much of the indigenous workforce, Europeans turned to enslaved Africans, and the transatlantic slave trade forcibly carried roughly 12 million Africans across the Atlantic over the following centuries.

The Columbian Exchange reshaped environments. Monoculture plantations growing a single crop over vast areas exhausted soils and replaced diverse ecosystems, Old World livestock multiplied and transformed American grasslands, and forests were cleared for cash crops, sometimes causing erosion and ecological damage.

A common error is reversing the direction of transfers. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chili peppers, cacao, and tobacco are American crops that went to Afro-Eurasia; horses, cattle, pigs, wheat, sugarcane, and deadly diseases went from Afro-Eurasia to the Americas. Native Americans did not give Europeans smallpox.

The Columbian Exchange is versatile exam evidence, relevant to prompts on the environmental effects of connection, demographic and population change, the causes of the Atlantic slave trade, the rise of plantation economies, and the consequences of exploration in the period c. 1450–1750.

Old World diseases devastated the Americas but American diseases did not devastate Europe because Afro-Eurasia had most of the world's domesticated herd animals and dense, connected cities, breeding crowd diseases to which its peoples grew partly resistant over centuries. The Americas had fewer herd animals and no such arsenal.

The Columbian Exchange marks the start of humans reshaping the planet's biology on a global, intercontinental scale. It produced both gains in calories and population and catastrophic death, slavery, and environmental disruption, and analyzing it well means holding both faces together.
